photographs.prompt:
Edit the FIRST input photograph. One full-bleed photographic image, wide 2.098:1, same camera and composition for a print gardening book. INPUT 1 is the base photograph for this exact first step. INPUT 2 is a three-view contact sheet of REAL CAMERA photographs of the man in the scene: very important for reshaping his jaw and chin faithfully. INPUT 3 supplies his actual cool-weather clothing only. This is one Cornish late-autumn afternoon, outdoors after a light shower, with cool overcast soft grey light, slight damp sheen on a few leaves and the tarp but no pouring rain or puddles. The picture will be paired with a warm sunny view taken the following late spring.
Keep John kneeling on the grass on the right, lowering the final brick onto the near right hem of a flat fully opaque, ordinary dark forest-green woven tarpaulin. Match his two hands on the brick, the ordinary perimeter weights, the existing layout and perspective of the tarp, his charcoal jumper, dark blue jeans and work shoes. Keep the fence, its worn low wall and the tiny slice at far right of his glass greenhouse on a pale grey brick plinth. Same understated, matter-of-fact photograph with comfortable headroom. NO shed.
The owner asks for a proper established lawn. REPLACE ALL the sparse, coarse and muddy ground visible OUTSIDE the edges of the tarp and under the actor with dense, closed, lush short mown lawn, attractive but authentic Cornish grass, mixed fine blades close together. A living continuous carpet with no earth peeking through it, right up to the tarpaulin, visible in front, along each side and behind. A few discreet recognisable flat dandelion, clover or plantain rosettes growing low in that lawn, especially near a tarp corner, testify to the weedy area, not an overgrown meadow. Leave the cover intact, flat and fully covering the treatment area with no dead weeds arranged on it. Subtle late-autumn clues only e.g. a couple of small fallen leaves at the fence, subdued greens; don't drown the details or darken the face.
Correct John's likeness using the real close views in the SECOND input as the authority. Match the slimmer taper in his lower cheeks, the small softly rounded and slightly set-back chin, his short mixed grey beard following his skin, softer natural jaw-to-neck transition. In particular bring back the protruding lower outline relative to the lower lip seen in the base, so it doesn't jut forward, square off, or appear reinforced by a shadow or by a thick block of beard. A relaxed mature man concentrating on the brick, still the same John, his natural forehead, hairline, nose and expression. Keep the downward gaze but let sufficient three-quarter part profile be seen to read the actual jaw contour. Understated documentary realism, normal texture, one image only, no typography or collage.

Revise the FIRST input photograph into one polished, believable documentary photo for a practical British vegetable-growing book. Full-bleed 2.098:1 landscape, same garden viewpoint and location. The base composition (reference 1) accurately locates John, working rake, rectangular smothered patch, folded dark green heavy tarp and set-aside bricks at back left, weathered fence on the low masonry wall at back, and just a sliver of glass greenhouse on the pale brick base at extreme right. No shed, no greenhouse filling the frame. Keep these, and keep the actual action of the metal rake head reaching into the centre foreground. Do not use the base image's clothing, weather, lawn texture or jaw as the reference for those features. References 2 and 3 are genuine camera evidence: reference 2 has three close views of John's real face and its profile, reference 3 shows his actual warm-weather olive T-shirt and olive work shorts. No handheld cap or microphone/lanyard. Make the clothes visibly different from his winter charcoal jumper and blue jeans: warm-weather faded olive short-sleeved T-shirt, bare forearms and lower legs, practical olive/khaki shorts, brown work footwear. John appears lean/ordinary, not muscular. A mild sunny LATE-SPRING day several months after a cool, damp late autumn cover was laid. Use clear, gently warm directional natural daylight, shadows cast from bricks and rake onto the ground and highlights on the lawn. Natural colour, no orange grade, no sun rays. Place light on the face so the jaw is not picked out in a hard dark shadow.
The owner wants a healthy, noticeably denser lawn around the treated patch and MORE REAL WEEDS TO RAKE UP. All surrounding lawn (right by his feet, in front, to the left and behind) should be convincingly dense, continuous, mown fine green grass, no earth showing through it. A few fresh low clover or plantain leaves in the healthy grass are fine. The area UNDER THE REMOVED TARP IS DIFFERENT: keep its original rectangular footprint, dark undug earth largely visible. Scatter several recognisable smothered broadleaf weeds still lying flattened on the soil: dried curled toothed dandelion leaves, pale plantain rosettes and tangled brown creeping stems with a few visible roots. Put several broad wilted leaves and roots, not just straw or grass clippings, into a distinct modest loose pile caught up right against the rake head as he draws it toward himself. Show a partially cleared swathe of dark soil beside it so the reader understands what is changing. Soft drooping straw/tan leaves with some earthy brown tones, not healthy green plants in the smothered patch. No imported mulch, hay or oversized heap. Rake means a single wooden handle held naturally in both hands, one transverse garden rake head with teeth engaging the stems. John stands on the turf at right.
For John's face follow the real close photographs in reference 2 rather than the strong projecting chin in the base. His lower cheeks slim down towards a soft small rounded, modestly set-back chin. Follow the real angle and depth from lower lip to chin when his head is inclined, soft jaw-to-neck transition, close grey beard following skin, no squared or protruding wedge of beard. The owner particularly notices the chin profile. Retain his hairline and ordinary mature features. Angle the face just enough in natural three-quarter profile, looking at the rake, for the new likeness to read; no posed smiling portrait. The change in clothes, weather, lawn density and the broadleaf weeds should be immediately visible and natural even at printed size. Single photographic frame; no lettering, border or montage.
